title: Causal Relationships Between Screen Use, Reading, and Brain Development in Early Adolescents
authors: Li M, Zhao R, Dang X, Xu X, Chen R, Chen Y, Zhang Y, Zhao Z, Wu D

primary_models.name: Linear mixed-effects regression of NIH Toolbox cognition and CBCL syndrome scores on daily texting, social networking site, and video chat hours, fit separately at baseline and 2-year follow-up
primary_models.location_in_paper: Figure 2 heatmap, baseline and 2-year follow-up panels (p. 4); Results section 2.2 (pp. 3-4); full coefficients, SEs and p-values in Table S1 (Supporting Information, not bundled with the PDF). Methods only summarized in Experimental Section (p. 9) with details deferred to Supporting Information.
primary_models.design: Two separate cross-sectional analyses of ABCD data: one at baseline (ages ~9-10) and one at the 2-year follow-up (ages ~11-13). At each wave, screen use and the outcome are measured at the same wave. The authors treat associations significant at both waves as 'consistent' (Figure 2 right panel) and only carried those forward to Mendelian randomization. No pooled repeated-measures model and no wave-by-IV interaction is described in the main text. Each of the six screen activities and reading time is entered in a separate model per outcome (the figure reports one coefficient per activity x outcome); whether activities were entered jointly is not stated in the main text.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (release not stated in main text). Baseline analytic n = 7107; 2-year follow-up n = 4505 (Table 1, p. 3). Baseline age 9.87 +/- 0.62 years (follow-up 11.87 +/- 0.64). Sex: 53% male, 47% female at baseline (54%/46% at follow-up). Race at baseline: White 0.661, Black 0.137, Native American 0.005, Pacific Islander 0.001, Asian 0.022, Other 0.173; Hispanic/Latino 0.20. Household income <$11,999 0.28, $12,000-24,999 0.14, $25,000-49,999 0.23, $50,000-99,999 0.25, >$100,000 0.10 at baseline (follow-up proportions differ: 0.05/0.05/0.13/0.28/0.49). Parent college or more 0.86. Exclusion criteria are not described in the main text.
primary_models.iv: Daily hours of three phone/SM activities from the ABCD youth screen time questionnaire, each analysed as its own IV: Text = texting on a cell phone, tablet, or computer; SNS = visiting social networking sites; VC = video chatting. Units are hours per day (Table 1 reports M +/- SD in hours). Baseline: Text 0.19 +/- 0.42 (41% any use), SNS 0.09 +/- 0.31 (17%), VC 0.16 +/- 0.38 (36%). 2-year follow-up: Text 0.53 +/- 0.96 (67%), SNS 0.51 +/- 1.10 (45%), VC 0.33 +/- 0.77 (43%). The weekday/weekend weighting used to form daily hours is not described in the main text. The same models were also run for TVM, Video, Game, and reading time (not phone/SM; not extracted).
primary_models.dv: Five NIH Toolbox cognition scores (picture vocabulary, flanker, pattern comparison processing speed, picture sequence memory, oral reading recognition) and eight CBCL syndrome scales (anxious/depressed, withdrawn/depressed, somatic complaints, social problems, thought problems, attention problems, rule-breaking behavior, aggressive behavior). Higher cognition = better ability; higher CBCL = more problems. Whether NIH Toolbox scores are uncorrected or age-corrected standard scores, and whether CBCL scales are raw or T-scores, is not stated in the main text. No descriptive statistics for the DVs are given in the main text.

primary_models.equation: Outcome[i] = b0 + b1*ScreenActivity_hours[i] + b2..bk*covariates (sex, household income, parental education, others unspecified in main text) + random effect(s) (unspecified in main text) + e[i]; fit separately at baseline and 2-year follow-up for each activity x outcome pair
primary_models.estimation: Linear mixed-effects model (software not stated in main text). Significance defined by Bonferroni correction across tests (Figure 2 caption); only significant cells are colored and labeled with beta in Figure 2. SEs and p-values in Table S1. The coefficient is described as beta but, given magnitudes (e.g., -4.28 per daily hour), appears to be unstandardized. Associations significant at both waves were passed to one-sample Mendelian randomization (Figure 1, Figure 3). No sex or other interaction tests reported.

primary_models.name: One-sample Mendelian randomization of daily reading time on genetically predicted texting, social networking site, and video chat hours (ABCD baseline)
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2 (p. 8); Figure 6c (p. 7); Results section 2.4 (pp. 6-7); interpreted in Discussion pp. 8-9 as a displacement effect.
primary_models.design: One-sample Mendelian randomization using individual-level ABCD genotype data. Genetic instruments (SNPs) were identified by GWAS of each exposure phenotype within ABCD (Figure 1a). extraction_flags:
1) The Supporting Information (Tables S1-S10) is not in the PDF. M1 has 78 cells, and only the 23 significant ones have values. I copied those values from the cell labels in the Figure 2 heatmap; the figure is an image, so I read them off zoomed renders of the page. The other 55 cells are blank in the figure (not significant after Bonferroni), so their B is null. SEs and exact p-values exist only in Table S1. Someone with the supplement should fill these in.

2) The Results text and Figure 2 disagree in several places:
- Text x picture vocabulary: the text says -0.93 and -1.56. The figure shows -2.20 at baseline and -0.93 at follow-up.
- VC x picture vocabulary: the text says -2.11 and -2.64. The figure shows -3.18 and -2.11.
- VC x picture sequence memory: the text says -1.46 and -1.90. The figure shows -2.43 at baseline and a blank (not significant) cell at follow-up. The -1.46 in the figure belongs to VC x oral reading recognition at follow-up.
I entered the figure values and explained each mismatch in the cell notes. Check these against Table S1.

3) The main text does not list the LME covariates, the random effects, the software, or whether the DV scores are raw, T-scores or age-corrected. The only covariates named are sex, income and parental education (Discussion, p. 8). Because of this, SD_DV is unknown for M1 and its cells cannot be converted to d. The coefficients are called beta but look unstandardized.

4) M1 is two separate cross-sectional LMEs: baseline (n=7107) and 2-year follow-up (n=4505). I coded the IVs by wave so each cell gets the SD for its own wave.

5) M2 is the one-sample MR of Text, SNS and VC on daily reading time (Table 2). I treated reading time as a qualifying behavioral outcome; please confirm that eligibility call. Only SEs are printed, so CI fields are null. SNS p is printed as "0.000". Text has p=0.045 but is not bolded, so I marked it non-significant under the authors' Bonferroni rule. Its d conversion uses the baseline reading-time SD of 0.67, on the assumption that the MR used baseline data.

6) M3 is a single reverse-MR estimate with phone/SM as the outcome: picture vocabulary -> VC hours, B=-0.001, corrected p<10^-8. It comes from the text only. The MR analytic n and confounders are not reported in the main text.

7) Several analyses were excluded because the main text gives only a range or unlabeled plot points: the forward MR for Text, SNS and VC (Figure 3a), the mediation and two-step MR indirect effects (Figure 6b/6d, Tables S7/S9), and the LME of screen use on reading time (Figure 6a/Table S6). A coder with the supplement could add them.
